steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## 2D LMS FIR adaptive filters
- LMS adaptive filters: most common error measure, mean square error
- derived from 1D LMS main method: minimize output mean square value by adjusting filter coefficients
- primary 2D input signal d (ideal signal + noise component), reference input signal x
- N by N causal FIR filter, impulse response w
- filter output: y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2); j = iteration number
- error signal at j-th iteration: e_j=d(n_1,n_2)-\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)
- next weight matrix = present weights + change proportional to negative gradient of MSE: w_{j+1}(n_1,n_2)=w_j(n_1,n_2)+2\mu e_jx(n_1,n_2)
- \mu = scaler multiplier, controls rate of convergence and filter stability
- advantages: no matrix operations, no averaging or differentiation; convergence independent of initial conditions, converges for any initial value -> good in nonstationary images
- disadvantages: expectations won't converge to a fixed value if tracking ability kept; choice of μ application-dependent, tradeoff convergence speed / tracking ability / steady-state MSE

## 2D LMS IIR adaptive filters
- same basic idea as 2D LMS FIR, but IIR filter -> reduces filter order requirements
- difference equation: y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{M_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{M_2} a(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)-{\sum_{m_1=0}^{L_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{L_2}}_{(m_1,m_2)\neq(0,0)} b(m_1,m_2)y(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)
- y(n_1,n_2), x(n_1,n_2) = output and input; b(m_1,m_2), a(m_1,m_2) = masks of input and output
- error: e(n_1,n_2)=d(n_1,n_2)-y(n_1,n_2); d(n_1,n_2) = primary output signal
- minimize MSE E\{e^2(n_1,n_2)\} by updating weights to converge to optimum weight
- advantages: can satisfy prescribed frequency response (lower order)
- disadvantages: nonquadratic performance surfaces, local minima; may become unstable during adaptation -> stability monitoring needed

## Recursive least squares adaptive filters
- 2D RLS: apply 1D RLS along horizontal and vertical directions
- finds coefficients recursively, minimizes weighted least squares cost function
- unlike LMS (reduce MSE), input signal considered deterministic -> fast convergence
- advantages: fast convergence; image denoising more accurate than 2D LMS
- disadvantages: large amount of computation, esp. 2D / multidimensional

## Lexicographic ordering
- turn 2D problem into 1D problem
- simpler implementation; use extensive 1D literature and existing 1D algorithms

## McClellan transformations
- transformation function: 1D filter design -> 2D filter design
- 2D adaptive filters from existing 1D prototype filters
- vs direct approach: lower computational complexity, faster convergence
- needs a priori info to select transformation function parameters -> pre-constrained

## Block diagonal 2D adaptive filters
- scan signal through blocks, weight adjustment per block instead of per sample
- advantage: signal correlations along both dimensions
- downside: assumes higher local stationarity

steps.text:
## 2D Least Mean Square FIR Adaptive Filters

Least mean square (LMS) adaptive filters use the mean square error, which is the most common way of measuring the error. The 2D LMS adaptive filters come from the main method of the 1D LMS adaptive filters, where the coefficients of the filter are adjusted so that the output mean square value is minimized. The filter has a primary 2D input signal d and a reference input signal x. The primary input signal d is made of the ideal signal plus a noise component. The filter is an N by N causal FIR filter and its impulse response is w. So the output of the filter is

y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

where j is the iteration number of the adaptive filter.

The error signal e_j at iteration j is

e_j=d(n_1,n_2)-\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

To get the weight matrix at the next iteration, we take the present weight matrix and add a change that is proportional to the negative gradient of the mean square error. So for the two-dimensional LMS adaptive filter the coefficients are updated like this:

w_{j+1}(n_1,n_2)=w_j(n_1,n_2)+2\mu e_jx(n_1,n_2)

where \mu is a scaler multiplier which controls the rate of convergence and the stability of the filter.

Advantages: The TDLMS adaptive filter does not need any matrix operations, and it does not need any averaging or differentiation either. Convergence of the algorithm does not depend on the initial conditions, it converges for any initial value, so it performs well on nonstationary images.

Disadvantages: If we want to keep its tracking ability, the expectations of the TDLMS adaptive filter will not converge exactly to a fixed value. So choosing μ depends on the application, and it is a tradeoff between convergence speed, tracking ability and steady-state MSE.

## 2D Least Mean Square IIR Adaptive Filters

The 2D LMS IIR adaptive filter has the same basic idea as the 2D LMS FIR adaptive filter, but it uses an IIR filter instead, and this can reduce the filter order requirements. The difference equation of the two-dimensional IIR filter is

y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{M_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{M_2} a(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)-{\sum_{m_1=0}^{L_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{L_2}}_{(m_1,m_2)\neq(0,0)} b(m_1,m_2)y(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

Here y(n_1,n_2) is the output and x(n_1,n_2) is the input of the adaptive filter. b(m_1,m_2) and a(m_1,m_2) are the masks of the input and output of the filter. The error signal is

e(n_1,n_2)=d(n_1,n_2)-y(n_1,n_2)

where d(n_1,n_2) is the primary output signal.

The filter weights are updated so that they converge to the optimum filter weight, and this minimizes the mean square error E\{e^2(n_1,n_2)\}.

Advantages: IIR filters can meet the prescribed frequency response since they reduce the order requirements of the filter.

Disadvantages: The performance surfaces of adaptive LMS IIR filters are nonquadratic and they can have local minima. Also adaptive IIR filters can become unstable while they are adapting, so some stability monitoring is needed.

## Recursive least squares adaptive filters
- 2D RLS: apply 1D RLS along horizontal and vertical directions
- finds coefficients recursively, minimizes weighted least squares cost function
- unlike LMS (reduce MSE), input signal considered deterministic -> fast convergence
- advantages: fast convergence; image denoising more accurate than 2D LMS
- disadvantages: large amount of computation, esp. 2D / multidimensional

## Lexicographic ordering
- turn 2D problem into 1D problem
- simpler implementation; use extensive 1D literature and existing 1D algorithms

## McClellan transformations
- transformation function: 1D filter design -> 2D filter design
- 2D adaptive filters from existing 1D prototype filters
- vs direct approach: lower computational complexity, faster convergence
- needs a priori info to select transformation function parameters -> pre-constrained

## Block diagonal 2D adaptive filters
- scan signal through blocks, weight adjustment per block instead of per sample
- advantage: signal correlations along both dimensions
- downside: assumes higher local stationarity

## Recursive least square adaptive filters

2D recursive least square adaptive filters can be developed by applying 1D recursive least squares filters in both the horizontal and the vertical direction. RLS adaptive is an algorithm that finds the filter coefficients recursively so that a weighted least squares cost function is minimized. The RLS algorithm is different from the least mean squares algorithm, which aims to reduce the mean square error, because in RLS the input signal is considered deterministic. This is why the RLS algorithm converges fast.

Advantages: The RLS algorithm converges fast. Image denoising based on the RLS algorithm is more accurate than with 2D LMS adaptive filters.

Disadvantages: The RLS algorithm needs a lot of computation, especially in the two-dimensional and multidimensional case.

## Lexicographic Ordering

A convenient way to implement 2D adaptive filters is to turn the 2D problem into a 1D problem using lexicographic ordering. This makes the implementation simpler, and it means the large literature on 1D adaptive filters can be used, together with all of the 1D algorithms that already exist.

## McClellan Transformations

McClellan transformations use a transformation function to turn a 1D filter design into a 2D filter design. With this theory 2D adaptive filters can be designed from existing 1D prototype filters. This system has lower computational complexity and converges faster than the direct approach. But it needs some a priori information about the system so that the parameters of the transformation function are selected correctly, otherwise it does not work properly, so the system is pre-constrained.

## Block Diagonal 2D Adaptive Filters

Block diagonal 2D adaptive filters are another approach. The signal is scanned through blocks and the weights are adjusted for each block, and not for each sample like in traditional adaptive filters. The advantage is that signal correlations along both dimensions are taken into account. But it assumes the signal has a higher local stationarity.

The filter is an N by N causal FIR filter with impulse response w. Then the filter output is given by

y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

where j is the iteration number for adaptive filters.

The error signal e_j at the j-th iteration is defined as

e_j=d(n_1,n_2)-\sum_{m_1=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{N-1} w_j(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

w_{j+1}(n_1,n_2)=w_j(n_1,n_2)+2\mu e_jx(n_1,n_2)

where \mu is the scaler multiplier which controls the rate of convergence and filter stability.

Advantages: The TDLMS adaptive filter can be implemented without any matrix operations or any averaging or differentiation. The convergence of the algorithm does not depend on the initial conditions and it will converge for any arbitrary initial value, hence it gives good performance in nonstationary images.

Disadvantages: The exact values of the expectations of the TDLMS adaptive filter will not converge to a fixed value if we need to maintain its tracking ability. Therefore, the design choice of μ depends on the particular application and involves a tradeoff between convergence speed, tracking ability, and steady-state MSE.

## 2D Least Mean Square IIR Adaptive Filters

For a two-dimensional LMS IIR Adaptive filter, the basic idea is the same as for 2D LMS FIR Adaptive Filters, except that an IIR filter is used, which can reduce the filter order requirements.[2] The difference equation of the two-dimensional IIR filter can be written as

y(n_1,n_2)=\sum_{m_1=0}^{M_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{M_2} a(m_1,m_2)x(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)-{\sum_{m_1=0}^{L_1} \sum_{m_2=0}^{L_2}}_{(m_1,m_2)\neq(0,0)} b(m_1,m_2)y(n_1-m_1,n_2-m_2)

where y(n_1,n_2) and x(n_1,n_2) are, respectively, the output and input of the adaptive filter. b(m_1,m_2) and a(m_1,m_2) are the masks of the filter's input and output. The error signal is given by

e(n_1,n_2)=d(n_1,n_2)-y(n_1,n_2)

where d(n_1,n_2) is the primary output signal.

The mean square error E\{e^2(n_1,n_2)\} is minimized by updating the filter weights so that they converge to the optimum filter weight.

Advantages: IIR filters can satisfy the prescribed frequency response because they can reduce the filter's order requirements.

Disadvantages: The performance surfaces of LMS IIR Adaptive filters are nonquadratic and may have local minima. In addition, adaptive IIR filters may become unstable during the adaptation, so some kind of stability monitoring is needed.

## Recursive least square adaptive filters

2D Recursive Least Square Adaptive Filters [3] can be developed by applying 1D recursive least squares filters along both the horizontal and vertical directions. The RLS adaptive is an algorithm which finds the filter coefficients recursively to minimize the weighted least squares cost function. Unlike the least mean squares algorithm, which aims to reduce the mean square error, the RLS algorithm considers its input signal deterministic. For this reason, the RLS algorithm has a fast convergence characteristic.

Advantages: The RLS algorithm has a fast convergence property. The accuracy of image denoising based on the RLS algorithm is better than that of 2D LMS adaptive filters.

Disadvantages: The RLS algorithm needs a large amount of computation, especially in the two-dimensional and multidimensional case.

## Lexicographic Ordering

One convenient approach to implementing 2D Adaptive Filters is to transform the 2D problem into a 1D problem by lexicographic ordering.[1] This simplifies the implementation and makes it possible to benefit from the extensive literature available for 1D adaptive filters and to use all of the existing 1D algorithms.

## McClellan Transformations

McClellan transformations [4] can be used to transform a 1D filter design into a 2D filter design by means of a transformation function. This theory allows 2D adaptive filters [5] to be designed from existing 1D prototype filters. Compared to the direct approach, this system has a lower computational complexity and a faster convergence rate. However, to work properly it needs some a priori information about the system to correctly select the parameters of the transformation function, which makes the system pre-constrained.

## Block Diagonal 2D Adaptive Filters

Block Diagonal 2D Adaptive Filters are an alternative approach [6] that scans the signal through blocks and applies weight adjustments for each block, rather than for each sample as in traditional adaptive filters. The advantage of this kind of system is that it takes signal correlations along both dimensions into account. On the other hand, it assumes a higher local stationarity of the signal.
